{{image-1}}

When I say ‘love that should not be’, what am I referring to? I’m referring to the kind that’s taboo. Whether because of your family or your culture or your belief system. I’m referring to the kind that’s impractical. Which could be because of your social class or your location or your temperament. I’m referring to any and all love that for some reason or another fires alarms in your mind as the fire burns in your heart. For many or even one strong reason, your instincts tell you it’s not a good idea. And yet deep feelings remain. Though maybe a cliché example, my mind turns to Romeo and Juliet: a tragedy about two teenagers, two little specs in a grand familial and political feud, who risked (and lost) their lives to recklessly pursue a love whose duration was best measured in days. This is obviously folly. And yet many rational modern people do the same.

It is unsurprising that the overwhelming religious and philosophical opinion on this kind of love and its’ passion is to steer clear of it. That is wisdom, some say. To be mastered by anything is to your detriment in everything. And to many (especially westerners), this is appealing. We are independent, rational, steadfast in our beliefs. “I would never date this kind of person”, “I don’t understand how they’re still friends with them”, etc. And so we judge others who’ve made decisions we don’t understand with their love life. However, the truth is that none of us are as independent or strong willed or rational as we think we are. No one looks for this kind of love, it finds you.

I like Dante’s depiction of this love in his _Inferno_. It is a whirlwind, a tornado that lovers are swept up into, unable to be grounded and out of touch with reality. They themselves could be seen as the whirlwind (or maybe better said a ‘world wind’), that sucks up everything in their path and leaves it a waste, while all they can clearly make out is each other. If this love is so destructive, why does anyone pick it? Why choose to upheave your life (and the life of others) for that which you just found and had previously lived without? Because at the end of the day, it is still love. It feels like finding what you’ve always had. Like discovering a substance besides oxygen that you’ve needed to breathe. It feels like the presence of the present. The storm is not preferable, but it is bearable, so long as you can still clearly see your lover’s eyes; while you can hear them laugh over the roar of the wind; still make out their smile through the raging tempest. This love is great confusion; great pain. And yet also, it is simply great. What a strange thing it is to love.
